ai-at-work.title: Valor, Point72 back General Intuition at $6B valuation as AI startup pushes into robotics
ai-at-work.excerpt: General Intuition, the startup building a foundation model that trains generalized AI agents how to move through space and time, is in talks to raise at a $6 billion pre-money valuation from new inves
ai-at-work.dwp_take: General Intuition just landed a massive $6 billion valuation with backing from serious money like Valor and Point72, positioning itself as a bet on AI that can actually move around and understand the physical world instead of just processing text. For digital workplace pros, this matters because embodied AI and robotics are coming to offices whether we're ready or not, and understanding what these foundation models do will soon be table stakes for workplace strategy. The irony is we spent twenty years getting people to adopt Slack, and now we're going to have to train robots to use it too.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI is building AI agents for everything. Will everyone use them?
ai-at-work.excerpt: Inside the frontier lab’s push to bring AI agents from software engineers to the masses.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI is building AI agents that can handle tasks across different software and systems, aiming to move this technology beyond just technical users. For digital workplace pros, this matters because autonomous AI agents could fundamentally reshape how work gets done, from automating routine tasks to changing job roles and requiring new governance frameworks. The real question isn't whether these tools work (they will) but whether companies can actually manage them responsibly when half the workforce treats new tech like a loaded gun they found in the break room.

ai-at-work.title: Robotics AI startup Generalist reportedly raises $200M
ai-at-work.excerpt: Generalist AI Inc., a startup that develops artificial intelligence software for robots, has reportedly raised $200 million in funding. Axios today cited a source as saying that 8VC led the investment
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Generalist AI, a robotics AI startup, has raised another $200 million in funding led by 8VC, adding to its $400 million Series B round from June. This matters to digital workplace folks because AI-powered robotics will eventually handle physical tasks in office environments, from mail distribution to facility management, reshaping how we think about workplace automation. At this rate, Generalist will have more funding than some countries' GDP, which is either a sign of genuine promise or a reminder that venture capital sometimes mistakes enthusiasm for inevitability.

ai-at-work.title: Chip software automation startup Embedd raises $2.7M
ai-at-work.excerpt: Physical artificial intelligence chip infrastructure startup Embedd Ltd. says it’s ready to fix one of the most critical bottlenecks in the multibillion-dollar robotics industry after raising $2.7 mil
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Embedd, a physical AI chip infrastructure startup, just raised $2.7 million to tackle automation bottlenecks in robotics. This matters because as organizations automate more workplace processes, the underlying chip infrastructure becomes the real constraint, not the software layer we usually fret about. Turns out the future of workplace automation might depend less on your fancy workflow platform and more on whether the actual hardware can keep up with the demand.

tools-tech.title: Businesses must reinvent their processes and workforce to scale agentic AI adoption
tools-tech.excerpt: Only 15% of US-based organizations have reached scaled, orchestrated, multi-agent adoption, according to the latest Deloitte research.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Only 15% of US organizations have actually scaled multi-agent AI across their operations, which means 85% are still stuck in pilot purgatory talking about AI while their workflows remain basically unchanged. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to understand that AI adoption isn't a technology problem, it's a process redesign problem, and you can't bolt agents onto broken workflows and expect magic. The real talk: most companies will keep throwing money at AI tools while their people work around them, because actually fixing your processes requires the kind of hard work that doesn't look good in a board presentation.

tools-tech.title: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back - here's why
tools-tech.excerpt: It's been a bumpy road for Mozilla's browser, but as the dust of doubt settles, Firefox has once again become my default browser on all platforms.
tools-tech.dwp_take: A tech journalist switched back to Firefox after abandoning it, impressed enough by recent improvements to make it their default across devices. This matters because browser choice directly impacts employee productivity, security posture, and IT support costs across organizations. Look, if Firefox is finally shipping features that make people voluntarily come back instead of grudgingly tolerating it, that's actually worth paying attention to, because desktop real estate is precious and browser wars aren't just nerdy theater.

tools-tech.title: 6 tips for better research with Microsoft Copilot
tools-tech.excerpt: Copilot, Microsoft’s generative AI chatbot, can do many things, but one of its best uses is as a researcher, for pretty much anything you want in business or personal use. If you’re looking for in-dep
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft published a guide on squeezing better research results out of Copilot by moving beyond lazy prompting. This matters because your team is already using these tools whether you've blessed it or not, so understanding how to actually use them properly beats pretending the problem doesn't exist. Here's the thing though: if your researchers need a six-step guide just to ask an AI a decent question, maybe we should all spend less time chasing the shiny new tech and more time training people how to think critically in the first place.

digital-culture.title: Prediction markets let you bet on layoffs. Do the masses think your company is next?
digital-culture.excerpt: Prediction markets let users bet on everything from sporting events to natural disasters and the outcomes of war. But they also set odds on layoffs and staff reductions at some of the largest companie
digital-culture.dwp_take: Prediction markets are now letting people bet real money on which companies will lay people off and how many, creating publicly visible odds on corporate downsizing. This matters because if your company's layoff odds are trading high on these platforms, your colleagues and the market are signaling they think cuts are coming, which could affect morale and your career planning. The dark humor here is that we've finally found a way to monetize workplace anxiety, so at least someone's making money off your existential dread.

digital-culture.title: AOC is freezing her eggs. Her choice can have a huge, positive impact for working women
digital-culture.excerpt: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is freezing her eggs, and she’s doing it in public. On Instagram, she filmed herself giving the first hormone injection, told her followers not to squirm, and answered the que
digital-culture.dwp_take: AOC publicly documented her egg freezing process on Instagram, showing the injections and answering questions about cost, timing, and procedure details that most women navigate in silence. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it's a direct challenge to the stigma that keeps reproductive health choices hidden from employers and colleagues, which ultimately affects how companies design benefits and culture. Honestly, watching a politician normalize a medical procedure on social media is more subversive than most corporate DEI initiatives will ever be, and it costs exactly nothing.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Exchange Server SE CU1 Delayed Amid AI-Assisted Security Reviews
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft has yet to set a firm Exchange Server SE CU1 release date as engineers work through AI-assisted security findings and ongoing patch releases. The post Microsoft Exchange Server SE CU1 Delaye
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft is pushing back the Exchange Server SE CU1 release while they wade through security issues flagged by AI tools and manage ongoing patch work. This matters because Exchange still powers email infrastructure at most enterprises, and delays in critical updates create uncertainty in IT planning and extend the window where known vulnerabilities sit unpatched. I'll believe the AI is actually improving security when we stop needing emergency patches every other Tuesday, but at least they're being transparent about the hold-up.

industry-news.excerpt: ChatGPT for Teens adds stronger protections for users ages 13 to 17, but parents still face limits around monitoring, age prediction, and AI safety. The post ChatGPT for Teens Adds New Safeguards — bu
industry-news.dwp_take: OpenAI rolled out ChatGPT for Teens with improved safety features for users aged 13 to 17, though monitoring and age verification still have real limitations. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because it signals how AI tools will eventually land in your actual workplace where younger employees and interns will use them, and your governance frameworks need to be ready before that happens. Here's the thing: we're always one step behind on AI safety, which means your workplace policies should assume the guardrails will fail and plan accordingly.
